Archimedes Quadruplets

GeometryCirclesArea
What it shows: A big half-circle holding two smaller ones, with four little circles tucked against its arc.
How to play: Drag the three dots along the bottom line, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Press a button to move the middle dot or start again.
Look for the math

Move the middle dot and every circle changes size. Yet the four small circles always have exactly the same radius and area as the two dashed twin circles. Why must that be true?

Three semicircles

The big semicircle has diameter AB, and the two small ones have diameters AC and CB. Write their radii as r1 and r2. Then the radius of the big one is

r = r1 + r2

Book of Lemmas, Proposition 5, gives the common radius of Archimedes' two twin circles:

t = r1 × r2 / (r1 + r2)

Power's four circles

Let O be the centre of the big semicircle, and D the top of the left small one. The horizontal step from O to O1 is r2 and the vertical step is r1, so the Pythagorean theorem gives

OD² = r1² + r2²

Two circles of radius x touch the line OD at D and touch the big arc at K. Their centres are x from D at right angles to OD, so

OL² = x² + OD² = x² + r1² + r2²

Because each circle is tangent inside the big one, OL = r − x. Squaring and cancelling x² leaves 2x(r1 + r2) = 2r1r2, so

x = r1 × r2 / (r1 + r2) = t

The same construction at E gives two more. The logic test checks this at a thousand positions of C and a thousand random drags, including that every circle really touches its line at D or E and its dot K lies on the big arc.

Equal areas

A circle's area depends only on its radius. Since x = t, each of Power's four circles has area πx², exactly the area of either twin; all four together cover 4πx². The radius is largest when C is halfway along AB, where x = r/4, and tends to zero as C approaches an end.

About the original

The Java applet drew the same three semicircles and four small circles, with a checkbox for the point names; its "about" text was a leftover from a polygon applet. The cut-the-knot article it came from now shows a GeoGebra figure rather than the Java program, so this port cites that article, which states and proves the equal-radius claim exactly. One applet detail is deliberately not copied: its helper circle was built with radius |AB| = 2r while the drawn arc has radius r, making its four circles half the stated size and its tangency dots miss the arc. Here the article's algebra is followed. Its unused TangentPoint and Other methods are harmless leftovers.

Press C in the middle, then drag C close to A. Watch the four circles shrink together with the twins, while the two radius numbers in the status line stay equal.
